projects.subject: economics
projects.title: The Two Inflations
projects.mission: The government reports that prices rose by 5.95%, yet low-income workers insist their cost of living has risen much more and their wage rise is no longer enough. Investigate the price index data, explain the gap, measure the loss in purchasing power, and choose a support policy within the finance ministry's budget.

learningCapsule.title: Index Numbers, Weights and Real Wages

sections.title: Weighted price index
sections.content: A price index combines the price changes of many goods into one number. Each good is given a weight equal to its share of the budget. Index = Σ(weight × price index of the good) ÷ Σ(weights). A base year has an index of 100.

sections.title: Why different households experience different inflation
sections.content: Prices are the same for everyone, but budget shares are not. A household that spends a large share on food feels food price changes much more than a household that spends a small share. The official index uses average weights, so it can hide the experience of particular groups.

sections.title: Nominal and real wages
sections.content: A nominal wage is the money received. A real wage is what it can buy: real wage = nominal wage ÷ price index. If prices rise by a larger percentage than the wage, the worker's purchasing power falls even though the wage went up.

levels.title: Find the Source of the Gap

questions.prompt: The official price index shows 5.95% inflation, while low-income workers report much higher inflation. The price data is the same for everyone. Which feature of the basket data best explains the gap?
options: Food has the largest price rise and a much bigger weight in the low-income budget.
Low-income households pay higher prices for every item.
Housing prices fell for low-income households.
The official index ignores food prices completely.
questions.answer: Food has the largest price rise and a much bigger weight in the low-income budget.
questions.explanation: The price index column is the same for all households. Food rose the most (index 114) and has a weight of 55 in the low-income basket versus 30 in the official basket, so food inflation counts much more in the low-income index.
hints: Compare the price index column with the two weight columns.
Which item rose the most, and how large is its weight for each group?

questions.prompt: Suppose food prices had not risen at all (food index 100) while every other price index stayed as given. Which index would fall by more?
options: The low-income household's index, because food has a larger weight in its budget.
The official index, because it covers the whole economy.
Both would fall by exactly the same amount.
questions.answer: The low-income household's index, because food has a larger weight in its budget.
questions.explanation: With food at 100, the low-income index would be (5500 + 4620) ÷ 100 = 101.2, a fall of 7.7 points from 108.9. The official index would be about 101.75, a fall of about 4.2 points from 105.95.
hints: Changing one price index has a larger effect on households where that item has a larger weight.

levels.evidenceUse: Use cpi_baskets.csv to compare the price changes and budget weights.
levels.simulationUse: Switch between the official and low-income baskets in the simulation and change the food price.

levels.title: Measure Both Inflations

questions.prompt: Using the official weights and the current price index of each item, what is the official price index?
hints: Multiply each item's weight by its price index.
Add them and divide by the total of the weights.

questions.prompt: Using the low-income weights and the same price indices, what is the low-income household price index?
hints: Use the same method as before but with the low-income weight column.

questions.prompt: A low-income worker's wage rose by the percentage stated in the field note over the same period. By roughly what percentage did the worker's purchasing power (real wage) fall?
questions.explanation: The wage index is 106 and the household price index is 108.9. Real wage index = 106 ÷ 108.9 × 100 ≈ 97.3, a fall of about 2.7%.
hints: Real wage is the nominal wage divided by the price index.
Compare the real wage index with its starting value of 100.

levels.evidenceUse: Take the weights and price indices from cpi_baskets.csv and the wage rise from field_survey_note.txt.
levels.simulationUse: Check your two index values and the real-wage change against the simulation readouts.

levels.title: Test a Price Policy

questions.prompt: Policy A lowers the food price index from 114 to 110 and leaves other prices unchanged. What is the low-income household price index after Policy A?
hints: Replace only the food price index and recalculate with the low-income weights.

questions.prompt: The worker's wage index is 106. Does Policy A fully protect the worker's purchasing power?
options: No. The price index of 106.7 is above 106, so purchasing power still falls slightly.
Yes. Any fall in the price index fully protects purchasing power.
Yes. The price index of 106.7 is below the wage index of 106.
No. Policy A makes purchasing power fall by more than before.
questions.answer: No. The price index of 106.7 is above 106, so purchasing power still falls slightly.
questions.explanation: Purchasing power is protected only if the price index is at or below the wage index. Since 106.7 is above 106, the real wage is still about 0.7% lower than before, although much better than the original 108.9.
hints: Compare the new price index with the wage index.
Purchasing power is protected only when prices have not risen faster than the wage.

questions.prompt: What is the highest food price index for which the low-income price index stays at or below the wage index of 106? Keep every other price index unchanged.
questions.explanation: The non-food part of the index contributes 2060 + 1040 + 510 + 1010 = 4620. We need (55F + 4620) ÷ 100 ≤ 106, so 55F ≤ 5980 and F ≤ 108.73.
hints: Write the low-income index with the food price index as an unknown.
Set it equal to the wage index and solve.

levels.evidenceUse: Use cpi_baskets.csv and the wage rise in field_survey_note.txt.
levels.simulationUse: Lower the food price index in the simulation and find where the low-income real wage stops falling.

levels.title: Choose the Support Policy

questions.prompt: Instead of a price policy, the ministry considers a wage correction. A low-income worker's base monthly wage is stated in the field note. After the wage rise, how much extra per month is needed to fully restore the original purchasing power against the low-income price index of 108.9?
questions.explanation: The wage needed is 12,000 × 1.089 = ₹13,068. After the 6% rise the worker earns 12,000 × 1.06 = ₹12,720. The extra needed is 13,068 − 12,720 = ₹348 per month.
hints: Find the wage that would keep the same buying power at the new price index.
Subtract the wage the worker already receives after the rise.

questions.prompt: The ministry must keep the low-income price index at or below the wage index of 106 and spend no more than the budget stated in the field note. Which policy should be approved?
options: Policy A: cut the food price index to 110 (₹800 crore)
Policy B: cut the food price index to 108 (₹1,200 crore)
Policy C: cut the food price index to 104 (₹2,000 crore)
Policy D: cut the housing price index to 100 (₹300 crore)
questions.answer: Policy B: cut the food price index to 108 (₹1,200 crore)
questions.explanation: Policy A gives a low-income index of 106.7, still above 106. Policy B gives (5940 + 4620) ÷ 100 = 105.6, within the target and within the budget. Policy C gives 103.4 and meets the target but costs ₹2,000 crore, above the ₹1,500 crore budget. Policy D reduces the housing index, which has a weight of only 20, and gives 108.3, still above 106.
hints: Calculate the low-income index under each policy.
Reject any policy that misses the target index or exceeds the budget.

levels.evidenceUse: Use policy_options.csv for the options and field_survey_note.txt for the wage and budget limit.
levels.simulationUse: Apply each policy in the simulation and check the low-income index and the cost before deciding.

requiredEvidence.instruction: Read every required file and use its information while solving the mission. The evidence is part of the investigation.

files.purpose: Compare the budget weights of the official basket and the low-income basket, and the current price index of each item.
Read the workers' complaint, the wage rise, the base wage and the finance ministry's budget limit.
files.content: Field survey of low-income workers: they report that their cost of living has risen far more than the official 5.95%. Their wages rose by 6% over the same period. Base monthly wage of a typical low-income worker: ₹12,000. Finance ministry budget limit for any cost-of-living support policy: ₹1,500 crore.

files.purpose: Compare the price index each policy would produce and what it costs.

requiredSimulation.description: Interactive economics simulation of a household price index. Controls: household type (official or low-income), price index of each item and a wage rise. It displays the weighted price index, inflation rate, real wage change and policy cost, and shows how each item's weight contributes to the index.
requiredSimulation.integrationComment: Use the simulation to see how the same price changes produce different inflation for different households, to measure the real wage, and to test each support policy against the target index and the budget.
